examples.knowledge_point: Finding an Expression for the Rate of Change of a Side Length Given the Rate of Change of the Area
examples.problem: The area of a square decreases at a rate of $20 \text{ cm}^2\text{/s}.$ If $x$ and $A$ denote the side length and area of the square respectively, then find an expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds.
examples.worked_solution:
This situation is different. Here, the *area* is changing at a constant rate,  and we want to know the rate at which the side lengths are changing.

First, let's draw a diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/f4125cebd7553bb8b106a8baff39a6e4a120b9d9e5cdf2c4c9c0a9a676558897.png)

We want to find $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}.$ The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A = x^2.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We know from the given information that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-20\text{ cm[math]^2[/math]/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this information, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-20 & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{10}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/4635202babbeec1f2308d624b5b3a8661f64a013e67b2df31f390da53ee17dcd.png)

The sides of a square are decreasing in length at a rate of $5\text{ m/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the square decreasing when the sides are $1\text{ m}$ long?
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $5\,\text{m/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-5.$ Also, when the sides are $1\,\text{m},$ we have $x=1.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =(-5)\cdot 2(1)=-10{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square decreases at $10\,{\text{m}}^{2}/\text{s}.$
